options: An XML-based protocol that exchanges signed assertions between an identity provider and a service provider
A type of firewall rule
A password hashing algorithm
A JSON-based protocol built on OAuth 2.0
questions.explain: SAML stands for Security Assertion Markup Language — an XML-based protocol built around signed assertions.

questions.q: What is OIDC built on top of?
options: It is not built on any other protocol
SAML 1.0
OAuth 2.0, with an added identity layer using ID tokens
LDAP directly
questions.explain: OpenID Connect (OIDC) adds an identity layer, including the ID token, on top of the OAuth 2.0 authorization framework.

questions.q: In a SAML login flow, what does the service provider (SP) actually validate to decide whether to trust the user's identity?
options: Nothing — SPs trust any assertion automatically
The digital signature on the assertion sent back by the identity provider
The user's IP address only
The user's password, which the SP checks directly
questions.explain: The SP never sees a password — it validates the IdP's digital signature on the assertion and trusts the claims inside it.

questions.q: What does an OIDC ID token contain?
options: An XML assertion
A signed JWT with claims about the authenticated user, such as issuer, subject, and expiration
Nothing — ID tokens are empty by design
The user's plaintext password
questions.explain: An ID token is a signed JWT whose decoded payload contains claims like iss, sub, aud, email, and exp.

questions.q: Why do many modern web and mobile apps default to OIDC rather than SAML?
options: Because OIDC is older than SAML
Because its lighter JSON-over-REST shape works naturally with mobile and API-first apps
Because SAML has been officially discontinued
Because OIDC does not require any authentication
questions.explain: OIDC's JSON/REST shape is lighter than SAML's XML and browser-POST redirects, which fits mobile and API-based apps better.
